label: Signal Processing and Optimization
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 315 to 358 and reframes a scattered list of signal methods as one idea: each technique chooses coordinates, constraints, a metric, or a score that exposes hidden structure. We preview PCA, ICA, NMF, sparse paths, barrier geometry, and proper scores as a single geometric program before opening each in turn.

label: One Geometry, Six Methods
notes: The common thread is representation choice. Ask four questions of every method: what object is represented, which transformations remain ambiguous, which constraint defines the feasible region, and which invariant certifies the picture. These questions turn persuasive plots into checkable claims and prevent us from trusting a figure that quietly violates a constraint.

label: PCA and Whitening
notes: PCA reads second-order geometry: the covariance draws an ellipse whose eigenvectors are principal axes and whose eigenvalues are squared axis lengths. Whitening rescales the cloud to identity covariance, turning the ellipse into a unit circle. That is the ideal pre-processing for ICA but also exposes the rotational danger we meet next.

label: Online Principal-Axis Learning
notes: An online eigenvector update keeps its state on the unit circle, so learning is a trajectory on a manifold rather than free Euclidean drift. We track the angle error as data streams in. Stronger covariance anisotropy makes the metric ellipse easy to draw yet can slow convergence for unlucky step sizes.

label: ICA: A Rotation Remains
notes: After whitening the covariance is identity, so PCA expresses no further preference. ICA demands independent coordinates, which covariance alone cannot detect. In two dimensions the entire remaining search is one rotation angle. A non-Gaussian contrast score selects that angle, recovering the original independent source axes from the linearly mixed observations.

label: The Gaussian Failure Mode
notes: Non-Gaussian sources carve preferred directions into the data, so the fourth-moment contrast has a sharp optimum. Two Gaussian sources flatten the contrast: every rotation has identical covariance and identical Gaussian marginals, so the rotation is unidentifiable. This failure mode is the cleanest demonstration of why ICA fundamentally needs non-Gaussianity.

label: NMF: Positive-Cone Geometry
notes: NMF drops orthogonality and independence and demands non-negativity instead. Data, basis rays, and activations all live in the non-negative cone, so a valid factorization is built from additive parts only. Multiplicative updates make this visible: multiplying by non-negative ratios can never turn a positive factor negative, protecting the cone.

label: Sparse Models: The L1 Diamond
notes: Sparsity constrains the solution to an L1 ball, which in two dimensions is a diamond. The exact answer projects the unconstrained optimum onto that polygon under the quadratic loss metric. Radial Euclidean shrinkage is a tempting shortcut, but when the metric is anisotropic it lands at the wrong vertex and the objective gap grows.

label: Bregman and Mirror Descent
notes: Mirror descent runs gradient steps in dual coordinates produced by a convex potential, then maps back through its gradient. The proximal step minimizes a linearized loss plus a Bregman divergence, so the geometry of the potential, not the Euclidean metric, controls the trajectory. Natural gradient is the Fisher-metric instance of this scheme.

label: Barrier-Induced Dual Geometry
notes: A logarithmic barrier supplies both a metric, through its Hessian, and dual coordinates, through its gradient. The central path minimizes a weighted cost plus the barrier. In primal coordinates it bends toward the boundary, yet in dual coordinates eta equals grad psi it is the straight ray eta equals minus t c, exactly the dual-flat picture.

label: Proper Scores and Hyvarinen
notes: A proper score makes estimation a game against Nature: the true distribution should minimize the expected score. The Hyvarinen score uses derivatives of the log density rather than its normalizer, so unnormalized models are scored directly. Its divergence equals half the expected squared difference of score fields, an identity we verify numerically.

label: Takeaways and Invariants
notes: Six methods, one habit: name the object, the residual ambiguity, the feasible constraint, and the certifying invariant. The closing checks are part of the lesson. Whitening must give identity covariance, demixing must recover independence only when non-Gaussian, NMF factors must stay non-negative, and the Hyvarinen score must satisfy its field identity.
